h1: Ultrasonic Pipe Thickness Testing: UT Pipe Wall Surveys Across the United States
html:
Ultrasonic pipe thickness testing is how a process plant, power station or mill finds out how much wall its piping has left. Atlantis NDT sends ultrasonic technicians to your site anywhere in the United States, takes straight-beam wall readings at the condition monitoring locations you name, and returns a gridded thickness record that your API 570 authorized inspector or piping engineer uses to set corrosion rates and next inspection dates. To scope it, request a UT inspection quote with your CML list or isometrics.

What ultrasonic pipe thickness testing measures

A thickness gauge sends a short sound pulse through a coupled probe, times the echo from the far wall, and converts that time to inches or millimeters using the velocity of sound in the metal. For piping the job is almost always carbon steel, low-alloy steel, stainless steel or a chrome-moly grade, and the number that matters is remaining wall at a known spot, compared with what that same spot read last time. The method is one-sided: you do not need to open the line, drain it, or reach the inside surface. It is described in ASTM E797 and in ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797), and the practical rules for piping programs sit in API 570 and API 574.

It is worth being plain about what the number is. A reading is the wall under the probe face. It does not describe cracks, it does not locate a pit that sits a few inches away, and it does not tell you how fast the wall is thinning. The value of a thickness survey comes from repeatable locations, a controlled technique and a record someone can compare against the next survey. That is why the record, not the single reading, is the product. Atlantis does not calculate remaining life or inspection intervals; your authorized inspector or engineer does that from our data.

Where piping thins and where the readings go

Condition monitoring locations (CMLs) are chosen by the owner under the piping inspection program, and API 574 describes the damage patterns that guide the choice. In practice the readings cluster around a short list of places.

  • Elbows and tees: erosion and flow-accelerated corrosion concentrate on the outside radius of an elbow and downstream of a reducer or control valve, so a grid is taken, not a single point.
  • Injection and mixing points: chemical, water or caustic injection can thin the pipe a short distance downstream, and the footprint is wider than most people expect.
  • Deadlegs and low points: stagnant branches, drain legs and sump-side runs collect water and salts and corrode at the bottom of the pipe.
  • Insulated and cold-service lines: where insulation has been opened for corrosion under insulation checks, the exposed pipe is read on a grid that follows the stained or wet area.
  • Soil-to-air and rack-crossing transitions: a pipe that leaves a sleeve or a support is a classic external corrosion spot.
  • Straight runs: a small number of readings establish the general wall condition so that the elbows and tees can be read against a baseline.

Piping circuits for process units, utilities and power plants are covered by piping circuit inspection and CML thickness surveys, and this page describes the ultrasonic part of that work.

Technique: probes, calibration and surface condition

Most pipe wall readings use a dual-element probe, in which one crystal transmits and the other receives. The two elements are angled slightly, which gives good near-surface resolution on corroded, rough pipe and lets the gauge read thin wall with a clean back-wall echo. Single-element probes with a delay line are used where finer resolution is needed on a smoother surface or on small-diameter tube.

Before a survey the technician calibrates on a step block or a known-thickness block of the same material as the pipe, covering the range expected in the field. Velocity depends on the alloy, so stainless, chrome-moly and carbon steel are not interchangeable on the block. Calibration is verified at the start of the shift, whenever the probe or cable changes, and at the end, so a drift in the record can be traced. The method is written into an ultrasonic procedure that follows ASME Section V Article 23 and is approved by an ASNT Level III; if you need one written to your program, see NDT technical procedure development.

Surface preparation decides the quality of the data more than any other single factor. Loose scale, flaking paint and pitting stop the probe from coupling, and a gauge will happily display a plausible wrong number on a bad surface. Where the pipe is heavily pitted, a wire brush or flap disc pass at each point is normally enough; heavy blasting is rarely needed for readings.

High-temperature lines, coatings and insulation

Hot lines are a routine part of refinery, chemical and power work. Ordinary probes and couplant fail on hot pipe: the couplant boils off and the probe wears or melts. High-temperature probes and couplants are available, and the technician calibrates on a block warmed to a similar temperature or applies a correction, because the velocity of sound in steel falls as temperature rises and the gauge reads thick if it is not corrected. Hot work is also a contact-time job: the probe is placed, the reading is taken and the probe is removed. If your site classes a line as too hot for hand contact, tell us when you request a quote so the right probes and safety plan are planned in advance.

Many gauges can read through coating, but only in a measurement mode that has been verified against bare-metal readings on the same material. Where a coating is thick, damaged or poorly bonded, the sound path is uncertain, and we remove the coating at the point or document that the reading is through coating and by which mode. Insulation has to come off at each location, and your site arranges removal and re-installation. We do not drill or cut insulation jackets.

Codes and standards that drive the survey

In the United States the examination is driven by the code for the piping system and by the inspection program that owner builds around it.

  • API 570 and API 574: in-service inspection, repair and alteration of piping, and the inspection practices that describe CMLs, damage mechanisms and minimum thickness.
  • ASME B31.3: process piping, which is the design code behind most refinery, chemical and pharmaceutical piping and the source of design thickness.
  • ASME B31.1: power piping, used in steam and feedwater systems at power stations and many industrial plants.
  • ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797): the standard practice for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement.
  • OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119: process safety management, whose mechanical integrity element expects inspection and testing of piping to recognized practice.

The minimum required thickness, or t-min, comes from the design calculation and your own piping data; we use the t-min you give us to flag low readings in the report, not to decide whether a pipe may continue in service. For the API side of that program, the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record, and we provide NDE data that supports them; see API 570 piping NDE support.

What the thickness report contains

Contents of a pipe thickness report
ItemWhat you receive
Component identificationLine number, circuit, CML number and a sketch or isometric marking each location
Material and nominal wallPipe size, schedule, material grade and the nominal thickness used for comparison
Procedure and equipmentProcedure number and revision, gauge, probe, couplant, calibration block and calibration checks
TechnicianName, ultrasonic level and the written practice the qualification sits under
ReadingsMinimum and recorded thicknesses by location, with the grid pattern and any scanned area noted
ConditionsSurface temperature, coating or insulation state, and any reading taken through coating
ComparisonPrevious reading and the t-min you supplied, with locations at or near it highlighted

The comparison column is what turns a set of numbers into inspection data. The owner's engineer uses the history to work out corrosion rates; Atlantis supplies the readings in a form that drops into an inspection database or spreadsheet.

Planning a pipe thickness survey in the United States

Most piping surveys happen during turnaround or outage windows, when scaffolding is up and insulation can come off. Technicians are mobilized to the site for the agreed scope, and the usual site requirements apply: refinery and chemical plants often ask for a safety orientation, a gas monitor, and sometimes TWIC for waterfront terminals. Confined-space and permit-required work is controlled by the site. Plants on the Gulf Coast also plan around weather and heat, and surveys on pipe racks in summer usually start early in the shift.

Online lines can be read during operation where it is safe and the surface temperature allows. Many programs take a first pass on running lines, then close out the remaining CMLs in the shutdown. For turnaround context, see turnaround and shutdown inspection.

What to send for a quote

  • CML list, isometrics or piping line list with line numbers and sizes
  • Material, nominal wall, t-min and the last readings, if you have them
  • Number of locations and whether a single reading or a grid is wanted at each
  • Operating temperature range, insulation, coating and any painted or lagged areas
  • Applicable code or program (API 570, B31.3, B31.1) and the format you want the data in
  • Access: scaffold, rope access or lift, permits, TWIC or site badging, and the site address

Where we work in the United States

Piping surveys cluster where the process industries do. These city pages carry local detail for ultrasonic work:

  • Houston: the Ship Channel refineries and chemical plants, and the densest piping inventory in the country.
  • Baton Rouge: Mississippi River refineries and chemical complexes with long, high-corrosion process lines.
  • Beaumont: Golden Triangle refining and petrochemical piping on the Neches River.
  • Chicago: refining, steel and power piping across the Calumet region and northern Illinois.
  • Philadelphia: Delaware River refining and utility piping with older infrastructure.
  • Tulsa: midcontinent refining, pipeline terminals and process equipment.
  • Los Angeles: California refineries and port-area piping under state and local safety programs.
  • Pittsburgh: steel, coke and power piping in the Ohio Valley.

Industry pages show how the same method looks in each sector: refineries, petrochemical plants, chemical plants, power generation, pulp and paper mills and water utilities. The overview of the method is on the national ultrasonic testing page, and the ASME Section V thickness requirements are explained in this guide to ultrasonic thickness measurement.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 and Agreement State rules. We do not calculate remaining life, inspection intervals or fitness for service. Specialist techniques that scan for crack-like flaws or map internal corrosion are not offered on this page, and thickness gauging will not find them. If a line needs a different method, we say so instead of stretching the gauge to cover it.

Training your own technicians in thickness gauging

If you want your own team to take these readings, our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training cover thickness gauging, calibration and report writing under SNT-TC-1A, and the ultrasonic testing simulator gives trainees practice before they touch a live pipe. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel, so the course supports your written practice rather than replacing it. Refinery crews can also look at oil and gas NDT training.

faq.q: How accurate is ultrasonic pipe wall thickness testing?
faq.a: On clean, properly prepared steel a calibrated dual-element gauge reads to within a few thousandths of an inch. Accuracy falls on rough, pitted or hot pipe and where the probe sits on a coating, so the report records surface condition and technique at each location.

faq.q: Can you measure wall thickness through coating or insulation?
faq.a: Insulation has to be removed at the reading location by your site. Coating can be read through only where the gauge mode has been verified against a bare-metal reading on the same material; otherwise the coating is removed at the point, and the report records which was done.

faq.q: Do you test hot pipe while it is running?
faq.a: Yes, within the limits of the probe and your site rules. High-temperature probes and couplant are used, and calibration accounts for the lower sound velocity in hot steel. Tell us the line temperature when you request a quote so the right equipment is planned.

faq.q: What is a CML and who selects them?
faq.a: A condition monitoring location is a marked point or grid on a piping circuit where thickness is measured at every inspection so readings can be compared over time. The owner's piping program selects the CMLs under API 570 and API 574, and we read the ones you assign.

faq.q: Will you tell us the remaining life of the pipe?
faq.a: No. We record thickness, compare it with the t-min and the previous reading you provide, and flag locations at or near the limit. Remaining life and the next inspection date are calculated by your authorized inspector or piping engineer from that data.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a pipe thickness survey?
faq.a: Send the CML list or isometrics, line sizes and materials, nominal wall and t-min, operating temperature, insulation and coating details, the governing code, and site access requirements. Photographs of typical locations help us plan surface preparation and probes.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic thickness testing better than radiography for piping?
faq.a: For wall loss it is usually the more practical method, because it needs access to one side only and no exclusion zone. Radiography has strengths for weld and profile imaging, but Atlantis does not perform it in the United States and we say so up front.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic thickness readings find cracks in a pipe?
faq.a: A thickness gauge reads wall under the probe; it does not find cracks. If a crack-like indication is suspected, the next step is a different examination chosen by your inspector, and we can support that with magnetic particle or penetrant testing where it applies.

faq.q: How should the data be delivered?
faq.a: We provide a report with a marked sketch and a thickness table, and can supply the readings in a spreadsheet laid out by CML number so it drops into your inspection database. Tell us your preferred template when you request a quote.
